name: p0f
desc: Versatile passive OS fingerprinting, masquerade detection tool
why: Passive OS fingerprinting reads TCP/IP handshake quirks to identify machines you never talk to, a delightful door into how the network leaks identity.

brief.what_it_is: p0f is a passive OS and software fingerprinting tool. It watches TCP/IP traffic, often from as little as one normal SYN packet, and infers the operating system and software on both ends of a connection without sending any probes. It also reasons about application-level payloads such as HTTP requests, and reports things like uptime, network link type, distance, language preference, and NAT or proxy setups. Output is printed as text blocks per detection (for example os, dist, params, raw_sig, mtu, uptime, and http request), and it can run in the foreground or as a daemon with a real-time API for third-party components.
brief.why_it_exists: The author's framing is that p0f identifies the players behind incidental TCP/IP communications without interfering in any way, as an alternative to active tools like NMap that can be blocked, slow, unreliable, or set off alarms. The page lists uses such as penetration-test reconnaissance, routine network monitoring, detecting unauthorized network interconnects, abuse prevention, and forensics.
brief.how_it_works: According to the page, p0f uses an array of passive fingerprinting mechanisms and matches observed traits against a signature database. Its TCP-level checks rely on handshake quirks, such as the relationship between window size and MTU, and it reads HTTP request and response headers for application-level signatures. Version 3 is described as a complete rewrite with a new signature database, and the page notes that earlier p0f versions are reused in projects such as pfSense, Ettercap, PRADS, and the OpenBSD firewall.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers the current release (3.09b) for download, with older 2.0.x and 1.8.x releases available. The README was not fetched, so compile and configuration steps are unverified. The page says the p0f-sendsyn tool must be compiled from the supplied source to collect SYN+ACK signatures, and that a README covers it. It also says p0f can run in the foreground or as a daemon.
brief.standout: Passive fingerprinting from a single SYN is a clever way to learn about machines you never talk to. The author says many other tools either reuse p0f's TCP checks or use weaker methods, which makes p0f something of a reference point in the field.
brief.status: Quiet, with evidence of some age. The latest version named on the page is 3.09b, and the copyright line reads 2000-2014. The page also says the public demo no longer works because the server now sits behind a load balancer. I found no release date or commit history, so I cannot confirm current activity.
brief.caveats: The public demo is broken, according to the homepage. The page asks for new signatures, especially for SYN+ACK and older platforms, and says the database is minimal for some categories, so detection coverage is uneven. Neither the license nor platform support was stated on the page. The README and design document were not fetched, so details on build dependencies and supported operating systems are missing.
quotes: P0f is a tool that utilizes an array of sophisticated, purely passive traffic fingerprinting mechanisms to identify the players behind any incidental TCP/IP communications (often as little as a single normal SYN) without interfering in any way.

Common uses for p0f include reconnaissance during penetration tests; routine network monitoring; detection of unauthorized network interconnects in corporate environments; providing signals for abuse-prevention tools; and miscellanous forensics.

judge.reason: p0f turns ordinary network traffic into clues about operating systems and network paths without probing, making it a distinctive way to explore how TCP/IP leaks identity.

entry.title: p0f
entry.tldr: p0f identifies the operating system and software on both ends of a network connection by listening only, sometimes from a single SYN packet, without sending a probe.
entry.deeper_look:
p0f watches TCP/IP traffic and guesses what is on the other end. It reads the quirks of a handshake, such as the relationship between window size and MTU, and matches them against a signature database. It also reads HTTP request and response headers for application-level clues. For each detection it prints a text block with fields like os, dist, params, raw_sig, mtu, uptime and the http request. It can also report link type, distance, language preference and NAT or proxy setups.

The author's pitch is an alternative to active scanners like NMap, which can be blocked, slow, unreliable, or set off alarms. p0f never interferes: it only reads traffic that is already going by. The homepage lists uses such as penetration-test reconnaissance, network monitoring, spotting unauthorized network interconnects, abuse prevention and forensics.

The idea underneath is that every network stack has habits. Two machines following the same protocol still fill in the optional parts differently, and those differences leak identity to anyone listening. Reading a raw signature and seeing why it points to one OS is a good way into how TCP actually behaves on the wire.

Version 3 is described as a complete rewrite with a new signature database. It can run in the foreground or as a daemon with a real-time API for other components. The page says earlier p0f versions are reused in projects such as pfSense, Ettercap, PRADS and the OpenBSD firewall.
entry.install:
brew install p0f

Capturing traffic typically needs elevated privileges. The p0f-sendsyn tool for collecting SYN+ACK signatures must be compiled from the supplied source.
entry.whats_unique: It learns about machines from a single ordinary SYN, with no probing at all. The author says many other tools either reuse p0f's TCP checks or use weaker methods.
entry.caveats: The code looks old (copyright 2000-2014, latest named version 3.09b), the public demo is broken, signature coverage is uneven, and the brew formula lists no executables, so the install path is unverified.
